title: Virtual Functions, Polymorphism and Virtual Destructors
objectives: Declare virtual functions and override them correctly using the override and final keywords
Explain dynamic dispatch through the vptr/vtable and the pointer-or-reference precondition it needs
Use pure virtual functions to define abstract pricing interfaces
State why polymorphic base classes require virtual destructors and what happens without one
motivation: One pricing loop must value cash, futures and options side by side without type switches sprinkled through the hot path. Virtual functions give C++ exactly that: call through an Instrument& and the object itself decides at runtime which implementation runs. The price is one hidden pointer per object plus one rule you may never break, delete through a base pointer and the base must have a virtual destructor, or the code has undefined behaviour.

blocks.md: A variable has a **static type**, what the compiler sees, and, for a pointer or reference to a base class, the object behind it can have a different **dynamic type**, what was actually constructed. When a member function is declared `virtual`, a call such as `p->pv()` binds to the dynamic type: each polymorphic object carries a hidden **vptr** pointing to its class **vtable**, a table of function pointers, and the call goes through that table at runtime. Non-virtual functions bind statically by the static type. The indirection costs a couple of memory accesses, real money in nanosecond paths, revisited in the internals module, but it buys extensibility: new instrument types drop into existing loops unchanged.

blocks.caption: Prints 1042.5: each element runs its own pv(), selected at runtime through the vtable.

blocks.md: Writing `override` on every redeclaration makes the compiler verify you are genuinely overriding, same name, same parameter types, same const-ness. Without it, a signature typo silently declares a brand-new function and the base version keeps running: the classic polymorphism bug. `final` seals an override against further overriding, or marks a whole class non-derivable. Destructors participate too: `~Derived() override` is legal and common.

blocks.title: Dispatch needs indirection
blocks.md: Virtual dispatch happens only through a pointer or a reference. Calling pv() on an `Instrument` **value** uses the static type, and initializing that value from an Option slices it (next lesson). A `std::vector<Instrument>` for heterogeneous instruments is almost always a design bug; store pointers instead.

Appending `= 0` makes a function **pure virtual**: the base declares the operation but deliberately supplies no body, and the class becomes **abstract**, you cannot construct an Instrument, only derived classes that implement every pure virtual function. This is how C++ expresses an interface: a pricing engine written against Instrument works for any instrument type added next quarter with zero changes to the loop. A pure virtual function may still have a definition, invoked explicitly as `Instrument::pv()`, but ordinary calls dispatch to the overrides.

blocks.caption: The interface fixes the contract; the derived type supplies the math.

blocks.text: Virtual destructors: the rule you never break

blocks.md: Deleting a Derived object through a `Base*` must run the whole destructor chain, but the delete only dispatches dynamically if the base destructor is `virtual`. Otherwise the behaviour is **undefined**: on typical implementations only ~Base runs and the derived part is never destroyed, but the standard promises nothing whatsoever. Hence the standing rule: any class intended as a polymorphic base gets a public virtual destructor (or a protected non-virtual one, for bases that are never deleted polymorphically).

blocks.caption: Output: ~Derived, then ~Base, the full chain, in reverse construction order.
Anti-example, shown only so you can recognize it: deleting through a non-virtual base pointer is UB. Compilers warn (-Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor); the fix is virtual ~Base().
Every object of a polymorphic class pays one hidden pointer, the vptr, linking it to its class vtable. That pointer is what makes delete and virtual calls dispatch correctly.

guidedExercise.prompt: Define an abstract `Instrument` with a pure virtual `double value() const` and a virtual destructor. Derive `Cash` (value = amount) and `Future` (value = price x multiplier). Build a `std::vector<Instrument*>` holding Cash{50000.0} and Future{5312.25, 20.0}, loop to total the book, print it, then delete every element through the base pointer. Expected total: 156245. State why the deletes are safe.
hints: Pure virtual syntax: virtual double value() const = 0;
Put override on each reimplementation so the compiler checks the signature matches.
Which version of pv() does i->pv() call when the function is not virtual, static or dynamic binding?
What does delete through Base* run when ~Base is not virtual?

commonMistakes: Forgetting override and mistyping the signature, silently creating a new function while the base version keeps running.
Omitting the virtual destructor on a polymorphic base, making delete-through-base undefined behaviour.
Expecting virtual dispatch through an object value or a sliced copy instead of a pointer or reference.
Declaring the override with different const-ness or parameters and wondering why the base version is called.
Trying to instantiate an abstract class whose pure virtual functions are not all overridden.
Marking a static member function or a constructor virtual, neither can be virtual.
realWorldApplication: Market data and order-management frameworks dispatch on message and instrument type through virtual interfaces, so new products plug in without touching the dispatch loop, the Open/Closed Principle running in production code.
quantFinanceApplication: A portfolio pricer iterating a std::vector<Instrument*> and calling pv() on each element is the canonical design: instrument-specific math lives in overrides, and the book-level loop never changes.
summary: virtual turns calls through base pointers/references into runtime dispatch on the object dynamic type, via its hidden vptr and vtable.
Always write override so the compiler verifies the signature; final seals overrides or classes.
A pure virtual function (= 0) defines an interface; the class becomes abstract and cannot be instantiated.
Polymorphic bases need public virtual destructors: deleting through Base* without one is undefined behaviour.
Dispatch requires indirection: values slice and bind statically, pointers and references dispatch.

quiz.prompt: Given `Option opt;` and `const Instrument& i = opt;`, with `double pv() const` virtual in Instrument and overridden in Option, what does `i.pv()` do?
options: Calls Option::pv(), dynamic binding through the reference
quiz.explanation: The static type of i is const Instrument&, but its dynamic type is Option. Because pv() is virtual, the call dispatches through the object vptr to Option::pv().
price() is virtual and the argument is passed by reference, so b.price() dispatches dynamically to Derived::price() = 20. fee() is non-virtual, so it binds statically to Base::fee() = 1. Total 21.
The virtual destructor makes delete dispatch to the most-derived destructor: ~Derived runs first, then the base part is destroyed by ~Base, reverse construction order.

quiz.prompt: A polymorphic Base class lacks a virtual destructor. What is guaranteed when `delete basePtr;` destroys a Derived object?
options: Nothing is guaranteed, the behaviour is undefined
quiz.explanation: Deleting through a Base* whose destructor is not virtual is undefined behaviour. On common implementations only ~Base runs and the derived part leaks, but the standard allows anything. Compilers warn with -Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor.

quiz.prompt: Which of these are legal C++?
options: A static member function marked override
A pure virtual function that also has a definition
quiz.explanation: Destructors can be virtual and overridden (override is legal on them); final on a class forbids derivation; a pure virtual function may have an out-of-line definition called explicitly as Base::f(). Static member functions cannot be virtual, so override is illegal on them.

quiz.prompt: A book holds three Instrument* elements: Cash with pv 1000.0, Bond with pv 995.25, Option with pv 12.75, each overriding a virtual pv(). What is the printed total?
quiz.explanation: Each call dispatches to the element own override: $1000 + 995.25 + 12.75 = 2008.00$. The loop never knows the concrete types.

flashcards.front: What is a virtual member function?
flashcards.back: A function whose binding is decided at runtime by the object dynamic type, through its vptr and vtable, when called via a pointer or reference.

flashcards.front: struct Base { virtual int price() const { return 10; } int fee() const { return 1; } }; struct D : Base { int price() const override { return 20; } }; f(const Base& b) returns b.price() + b.fee(); what does f(D{}) return?
flashcards.back: 21, price() dispatches dynamically (20), fee() binds statically (1).

flashcards.front: Derived declares double pv() while Base declares virtual double pv() const. What silently happens?
flashcards.back: Different const-ness: Derived::pv() hides the base function instead of overriding it, so base pointers still call Base::pv(). The override keyword turns this into a compile error.

flashcards.front: What does a pure virtual function do to its class?
flashcards.back: virtual double pv() const = 0; supplies no implementation in the base and makes the class abstract: it cannot be instantiated, and derived classes must override every pure virtual.

flashcards.front: Why must a polymorphic base class have a virtual destructor?
flashcards.back: So delete through Base* dispatches to the derived destructor; without virtual it is undefined behaviour, typically only the base dtor runs and the derived part is never destroyed.
